newsitem.title: UK: Veteran Loony leader won't stand in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Veteran Loony leader won't stand in UK election.

text.p: Britain's longest serving political party leader, Screaming Lord Sutch of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, said on Thursday he would miss his first general election since 1963.

Sutch, Lord of Misrule on the British political scene, said he would be unable to contest the May 1 election because his 80-year-old mother was in hospital recovering from a hip replacement operation.
But Sutch, whose party campaigns under the slogan "Vote for Insanity, You Know it Makes Sense", did not expect to be out of politics for long.
The ruling Conservatives and the main opposition Labour parties were much closer together than suggested by Labour's 20-point opinion poll lead, he said.
"I'm not standing in the election because my mother is very ill," Sutch, 56, told Reuters. "I've got to visit her every day in hospital.
"But I"ve got a bet on that there will be no working majority and there will be another election in October or November. I've got 100 pounds ($160) at 20-1."
The Loonies are fielding about 30 candidates, but the exact number is not clear because some hopefuls around the country have used different party names.

Before he went into politics, Sutch ran a 1960s rock band called the Savages in which stars such as Noel Redding of the Jimi Hendrix Experience, Keith Moon of The Who and guitar legend Jeff Beck played early in their careers.
Sutch, who has become one of Britain's best-loved fringe candidates with megaphone, top hat and leopard-skin tailcoat, has stood unsuccessfully for parliament more than 40 times.
He would be doing some campaigning, but would not be standing in Prime Minister John Major's Huntingdon constituency.
"I think he looked on me as his lucky mascot," Sutch said. "He's basically a nice guy."
Loony policies for 1997 included provision of heated lavatory seats for pensioners and extending the Channel Tunnel to Guernsey and Switzerland to give Britain tax-haven status.
Sutch said he had originally set up his party for people who didn't want to vote, so he would consider himself the election winner if more people stayed home than voted.
"If more people don't vote, I will claim victory," said Sutch, who has also bet five pounds ($8) that he will become prime minister -- at odds of 15 million to one.
